title: Which game engines do you think going to dominate AI gamedev in the future?
author: _Vultrix_
selftext:
I’ve been thinking about how the game engine situation will change as AI tools are inevitably more powerful. I wanted to get the your guys thoughts on where things are heading. Do you guys think  traditional engines like unity, unreal, godot will stay dominant by adding AI plugins/copilots, or are they too bloated for AI gamedev. Browser based games are working great with AI through three.js and similar ones, so do you guys think that browser-based stacks taking off for quick AI-generated games? Or will we see a shift toward custom engines built specifically to interface directly with AI agents and dynamic generation?

Where are you placing your bets for the next few years? What stack are you currently using with AI tools? Do you think it's worth it to just choose an established game engine right now even if theres chance it 'falls off'?

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Everyone who's saying engines are dead or obsolete has not created anything beyond a vampire survivors level game.

Engines supply so many incredibly useful time-saving features it's absurd. Yes you could use AI to replicate them yourself, but every single one would require countless hours to implement, perfect, and debug to the same level. We're talking hundreds or thousands of hours each, even with AI's help. 

Yes you can have AI vibecode you a Fluid Flux, or a SpeedTree, or a Nanite or Lumen imitation, or a Metahuman and parametric clothing system. However to get to those actual levels of quality, polish and optimization is NOT easy, and you and the AI likely do not have the skills to do so because of the expertise required to be able to judge, for instance, the realistic root network distribution for speed tree, or the water splash  and flow physics, or whether the light bounces are accurate enough to make for realistic global illumination. It's absolutely hilarious that people think these features are worthless. Sure, if you are building a stylized game that relies on zero PBR, doesn't care about realistic physics, or maybe it's 2d, then the worth becomes less. If you're building a 2d deckbuilder with stick figure art then  yeah, there's almost nothing you're getting outside of the interface.

But any people reading this who think all an engine offers is an interface need a reality check and to go study up on game dev fundamentals so they don't end up unpleasantly surprised. Or focus on games that don't care about what IS offered by engines. Don't build an open world, realistic pirate simulator. Build a Comfy Top-Down Pig Survivors.

And to answer OP - at this point I'm sure UE and Unity will both continue to do well. I think Godot will be left behind. UE will be the go-to for realistic games, Unity for stylized and/or 2d. Or people will just vibe code their own engines for 2d or use Pixi as a framework or something (honestly most 2d games require so little resources that Pixi could end up becoming the go-to for any 2d physics/lighting/etc as a base. AI works incredibly well with it.

I think Unity could fall behind UE quite handily though if they don't offer a reasonable reason to use them over it. Once upon a time that was pricing. But  UE has such a good model now, especially for lower earners, that the argument to use Unity mostly comes down to recompile times, whether or not it has exclusive plugins you prefer, or i remember there being an instance with Unity's renderer where it can leverage more fully loaded npcs/objects on the screen at a time.  UE though can load something like 100x that many under different conditions though, so it just depends on your needs. Like whether you need 1000 vs 500 fully loaded or whether your games wants full FPS while the entire screen (going off into the far distance) is jampacked with them. Also if going higher poly, Metahuman makes for a very powerful architecture. However the metahuman pipeline is, imo, not really great for stylized actors. Often times you don't want them making the same facial expressions as realistic ones, and importing custom meshes can be tedious when you already have one you like (and then have to sculpt the metahuman mesh to it.) Hence why I think Unity will continue to be preferred for stylized games, though this could change if they expand metahumans to really help stylized character flourish on the same architecture. Especially with like customized expression offsets or something. If you could have extensible anime expressions (in terms of stylism) it could go hard.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
Are we talking about quickly bashed solo games only?  
  
Because as soon as you get team or get to a level where you need some outsourcing -  you need people to have familiar and common frameworks.   
  
Like if I was about to work with 3 or more people - lots of what I would do in solo dev with AI would not be applicable at all.   
I would need a huge change in how I work, what I document, to what degree I allow AI to improvise etc.  
  
The reason people like popular frameworks, is because you can describe results and tasks with highest precision to anyone who is using the same framework.   
And popularity means ease of collaboration and shared experience.  
  
This does not work with custom engine, because nobody knows what your LLM has generated there, without dedicating huge amount of time to learning it.  
And if you don\`t learn, and just try to improvise with agent and hope for the best, you gonna introduce lots of conflicts. And every single new coder on the team will increase the likelihood that we will run into something.  
  
Frameworks and engine navigate this by precise, updated documentation,  incremental changes, stable and predictable rules that people learn over the years etc.  


So yeah, as long as teams of developers exist - we absolutely do need an established engines and frameworks, because no one will consider your offer to "just learn my inhouse engine, bro", unless you are some big name in the industry.

replies.author: monsterfurby
replies.body:
I don't see how one-shotting will ever replace a certain amount of game design. The more detailed, the better. Yes, we're shifting away from formal code towards natural language, but logic is still logic, no matter how it's expressed.

Yes, sure, you now can develop a full game on your own, but you're not going to top out the quality ceiling. Game mechanics are still largely applied mathematics with a ton of editorial calls, and a thesis/desired mood/expression is usually carried through them in a way that GenAI will always struggle to realize because it defaults to the mean. And mean - that is, average - is not a term that usually matches with the intent of making a memorable piece of entertainment.

Quality control and playtesting need humans as well, and I would never discount the parasocial component of game development. People *do* want to engage with creators. Voice actors are of course the superstars of that interaction, but personalities like Hideo Kojima, Richard Garriott, Shigeru Miyamoto, Naoki Yoshida, or even indie devs like Ty Sylvester (Rimworld), Dan Salvato (DDLC) or Eric "ConcernedApe" Barone (Stardew Valley) are also definitely a reason people engage with their games over a long period of time. I'm pretty sure that putting less of themselves into the game, especially the game design, would have been poison for that kind of engagement.
